Later today we are having a firm-wide trader meeting at @smbcapital. A few teams and a couple handful of traders have been struggling. This aligns with what I’m hearing from other desks as well as those on the retail side.

Only fair for me to highlight both the successes AND the struggles of the traders I work with as I try to convey the authentic truth of being a trader.

On the SMB call we will discuss what has been working well, what hasn’t been, and how best to adapt. Soliciting feedback across teams and individuals.

Here is the main message I will be conveying to their traders which I think is useful for all to hear:

IMO, the most common issues I’m seeing is that traders are getting overly involved and over-allocating risk to situations that had potential but never unfolded optimally.

$BWET is a name that got extended, but never enough to take a real stand.

The breakouts in $QQQ or certain single-stock names had solid charts but the breadth beneath the market was awful. We still had yellow lights flashing in certain areas.

The recent AI sell-off was extended and had its moments, but it lacked the intraday flush or intraday setups to size into anything.

When these setups have unfolded suboptimally, traders have continued to stay involved and allocate risk in a refusal to acknowledge that the setup is not as good as it had the potential to be.

I’d argue this comes down to maintaining an objectively high level of subjectivity. Selectivity is staying in your lane and waiting for the setups in your playbook that match the current regime.

Unlike w poker, nothing is forcing you to play or to take a subpar setup. Essentially, you have a good hand and want to place a bet, but if the flop pans out suboptimally, you fold. A lot of traders have not been emotionally willing to fold and not play the hand.

Good trading is recognizing that there might be some positive signs, but then avoiding or sizing down when it doesn't fully line up.

Bond returns have become positively correlated with equity returns. And I expect that relationship to persist for one simple reason: bonds themselves have become a risky asset.

But that doesn't mean bonds will magically return to being a low-risk asset class offering decent positive returns and meaningful diversification.

Quite the contrary.

Pension funds and other investors abandoning French government bonds further confirm that the nature of bonds has fundamentally changed.

And when yields eventually decline, as I expect they will, won't the reason be yet another reminder that bonds need central bank support to prevent actual defaults?

I think so.

And in that environment, can you think of other asset classes that would benefit even more from that support than the bonds themselves?

We can!

That's why we build robust, long-term investment portfolios without traditional bonds, but with scarce assets such as gold.

Immigration policy must be driven by the present, not the past, and business leaders are too terrified of the left AND the right to acknowledge this.

Recent H1B discourse revolves around a longstanding immigration sleight-of-hand.  H1B proponents point to exceptional people who came here decades ago as if they represent the current state of the program in the same way that advocates for low-skill/illegal immigration point to very favorable immigrant crime/welfare/education/etc statistics that do, in truth, have them beating native-born Americans on many fronts.

It is all a sham.  The world that created those statistics, people, and businesses no longer exists.  Brilliant but desperate Vietnamese fathers who fled communism have nothing in common with young men from Honduras, and the crime rates/economic acccomplishments/integration of the former should not be used to justify mass migration of the latter.

Nor should the accomplishments of people who managed to get an H1B visa in the 90s (when the program was capped to just 65,000 visas) be used to justify staffing agencies and tech companies using the program to replace American jobs for less money.  The obvious abuse going on is politically suicidal and something that even the most ardent supporters of the visa should want to crack down on, no immigration program can possibly survive the obvious and widely known reality of what is going on.  I am a longtime outspoken advocate for stealing the best people from other countries to make our own better, runaway abuse of existing programs robs the government of the worker trust required to do so.

Lots of people in the tech space know this.  Even the dumb people are smart enough to see it.  Nobody actually believes these are all incredible people with unique talents performing jobs no American can. Or, more likely, both.  I know too many tech execs in particular who feel trapped, like the only winning move is to stay silent.

JD is blowing the whole thing wide open by putting facts and stats front and center that nobody wants to engage with.  Critics will talk about anything and everything else but these damning facts and this obvious truth, that H1B visas serve neither their original purpose, legal purpose, invented purpose, or the American people.

• Tesla's 2027 Megapack production capacity is nearly sold out.

•  Tesla plans to launch Cybercab service in Dallas in November 2026, followed by additional cities.

2. Pick one thing and commit.

One market. One setup. One risk framework. And don’t touch anything else for a year.

A mentor, a partner, a community. Someone who acts as your manager, coach and reality check all at once. Be comfortable making progress alone… but don’t shut out opportunities that help you hit your goals faster.

posts.text:
Very happy to share a new paper, “Technology Bottlenecks: Measuring Where AI Could Raise the Value of Work It Cannot Yet Do.”

AI exposure measures ask about the work AI is capable of doing. We ask instead where the marginal value of work AI cannot yet do may rise as AI speeds up the rest of the job.

To do so, we employ 288 million U.S. job postings mapped line by line to their closest O*NET tasks and GPT-4 feasibility ratings from Eloundou et al. (2024) to construct a measure, “bottleneck pressure,” for each task in each occupation that posts it. 

Using a simple task-based framework, we derive this pressure at the task level, showing that for an AI-infeasible task it is the exposure of the occupation that posts it, so the same task can face very different bottleneck pressure in different jobs.

Reporting bottleneck pressure alongside AI exposure shows both the scope for AI to perform work and where improving the work it cannot do may pay off more as capabilities expand.

We formally announced Mirendil less than 4 months ago. Today, I'm excited to share an important milestone for:

Pretraining at scale without a pretraining team.

Mirendil's mission is to solve Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) and use it to democratize frontier AI development, ultimately accelerating science and technology. At Mirendil, when we think about RSI, we think holistically about the company as an intelligent entity that self-improves toward its goal. From that perspective, the most powerful notion of acceleration is reducing the time and resources (number of human experts, compute, and other costs) needed to achieve ambitious goals.

Given that pretraining is perhaps the most important yet most challenging part of frontier AI development, we decided to run an ambitious controlled experiment: Starting fully from scratch, can we significantly reduce the time, number of human experts, and compute resources needed to go all the way to successfully pretraining a strong coding model at scale?

Mirendil-Base is the result of this experiment. Our first pretrained model was built by one researcher in 3.5 months, with less than $10M in compute. This includes all the research and small-scale experiments it took to get there, as well as the final training run.

The recipe holds up as the models get bigger. For reference, Mirendil-Base is in the 100B-500B parameter range, Mirendil-Base-Large in the 500B-2T range, and Mirendil-Base-XL in the 2T-10T range.

We're beginning to see a world where a single researcher, empowered by AI, can take on work that once required an entire research organization. As these systems improve, the bottleneck shifts from the size of a team to the ambition and judgment of the people directing them. This has profound implications for who gets to build AI and, ultimately, who gets to push the frontiers of science and technology forward.

We’ll share independent evaluations, post-training benchmarks and API-access sooner than you think so stay tuned!
